1352.title: The vowels
1352.hook: dots and dashes added by the Masoretes to show vowels
1352.howItsDone: Printed Hebrew Bibles and prayer books carry the vowel points, and children learn to read with them; the handwritten Torah scroll read in synagogue has no vowels, so the reader prepares in advance from a printed text that shows them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sofit: the five letters that change shape when a word ends. Your line: five endings. Today, a new week, and the little marks that make the letters speak.

Open a Torah scroll, the handwritten one kept in a synagogue's ark, and look closely. Black letters, row after row, beautifully formed, and something missing. No dots under the letters, no little dashes, no marks above. Just consonants. The person reading aloud on a Sabbath morning has to know how each word sounds before they get there. So the reader prepares, and one tool is a printed book in two columns: the plain letters on one side, and on the other, the same words with tiny dots and lines added. Those marks are today's word.
screen: `A TORAH SCROLL, UP CLOSE.` → `ONLY CONSONANTS.` → `A PRACTICE BOOK WITH THE MARKS.`

segments.voice: Nikud: the dots and dashes that show the vowels. Four ways in. First, the letters. Every letter in this block, from alef to tav, is a consonant, or a silent letter like alef and ayin. Hebrew can be written with no vowels at all; a reader who knows the language fills the sounds in. Second, the marks. Scribes and scholars called the Masoretes worked out small signs to fix how the sacred text was read aloud. A short line under a letter says ah. A single dot under it says ee. A dot above says oh. They sit around the letters without changing a single one; the marks only guide the voice. Third, why it matters. Some words share all their letters and differ only by vowels. Samech, peh, resh can be read sefer, a book, or sofer, a scribe. The dots tell you which. The Talmud, in tractate Nedarim, reads a verse from Nehemiah, where Ezra's helpers read the Torah to the people and "gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading," as pointing to the breaks and the chant of the text, the reading handed down with the letters. Fourth, where you'll meet them. These dots are scaffolding. Children learn with them. Prayer books print them. And a Torah reader carries them in memory, even when the scroll leaves them out.

Say each one quietly, then pick one and let it go on the out breath, the letter still while only the breath changes. If you pray, you can let one word of a prayer you know rest on your breath the same way.
Nikud. The vowel points: dots and lines around the letters, telling the voice how to read them. Today's word.
Your line: the dots. You already fill in more than anyone tells you. Rest well.

1353.title: First word: shalom
1353.howItsDone: Jewish children learning to read Hebrew sound out words letter by letter with the vowel points; shalom is used as a greeting for hello and goodbye, and in the longer greeting shalom aleichem.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nikud: the dots and lines that tell the voice how to read. Your line: the dots. Today, letters and dots come together into a whole word.

Four letters. For weeks they've arrived one at a time. Shin, the letter on the door. Lamed, the tall one that rises above the line. Vav, the hook, a single upright stroke. And mem, water, in the closed square it takes at the end of a word, one of the five endings. Today they sit down together, right to left, with two small marks to give them a voice. They make a word said at doors, written in letters, and found at the end of the priestly blessing. Your first Hebrew word, read on your own.
screen: `FOUR LETTERS, MET ONE BY ONE.` → `RIGHT TO LEFT.` → `TWO SMALL MARKS.` → `YOUR FIRST WORD.`

segments.voice: Shalom. Read it four ways. First, from the right. Hebrew runs right to left. Shin, with its three arms; the dot on its right arm says sh. On the left arm, it would say s. Under it, a small T-shaped mark that, in the pronunciation used in Israel, says ah. Sha. Second, the middle. Lamed, reaching up. Then vav, with a single dot right on top, which turns it into a vowel: oh. Lo. Third, the end. The closed square of final mem, which just says m. Sha, lo, m. Shalom. Fourth, where it lives. At the end of the priestly blessing in Numbers, the last words are "and give thee peace," and in Hebrew the last word is shalom. In the Psalms: "seek peace, and pursue it." In daily life it's a hello and a goodbye, and it begins the greeting shalom aleichem, peace be upon you. One word, used at the door coming in and the door going out. In a few days we'll open the root underneath it. For now the job is simpler: the letters, the dots, and your own voice putting them together.

If there's someone you'd say it to, bring them to mind as you say it; if you pray, you can hold the word for a moment as you sit.
First word. Shalom: shin, lamed, vav, final mem, the first Hebrew word you've read yourself, letter by letter. Today's word.
Your line: shalom, read. Four letters, two marks, and one word that is now yours. Until next time.

1354.title: Shema Yisrael
1354.hook: read the Shema's first two words in Hebrew
1354.howItsDone: Jews who keep the daily prayers say the Shema in the morning and evening prayers and again at bedtime, and a common custom is to cover the eyes with the right hand while saying the first line.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your first word: shalom, four letters and two marks. Your line: shalom, read. Today, two words, the first two of the Shema.

"Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." Up to now on this path, you've met that line in English. In Deuteronomy, the next verse says to speak these words when you sit in your house and walk by the way, when you lie down and when you rise up. So it's said at bedtime and in the morning service, and tradition places it on the lips of children and of the dying. In the prayer book it stands in Hebrew, and it opens with two words. Today they stop being sounds and become letters you can read.
screen: `HEAR, O ISRAEL.` → `LYING DOWN AND RISING UP.` → `TWO WORDS, IN HEBREW.`

segments.voice: Shema Yisrael. Read it four ways. First, shema. Right to left: shin, with its dot on the right arm, sh. Under it, two dots stacked, a mark that here barely sounds. Then mem, with a short line under it: ma. Then ayin, the eye, which says nothing. Sh, ma, and silence: shema. It means hear, or listen. Second, Yisrael. Yod, the small one, with a dot under it: yi. Then the three-armed letter again, but the dot has moved to the left arm. That makes it sin, which says s. Yis. Then resh with the T-shaped mark: ra. Then alef, silent, carrying two dots side by side: eh. Then lamed. Yis, ra, el. Yisrael. Third, a detail in the scroll. By scribal tradition, in a Torah scroll the ayin at the end of shema and the dalet at the end of the verse's last word are written larger than the letters around them. Some readers notice that together they spell ed, a witness. That's a reading, not the verse's plain meaning, and it's offered as one. Fourth, a gesture. The Talmud tells of Rabbi Judah the Prince passing his hand over his eyes as he said the Shema, and a custom grew from it: covering the eyes for the first line. The eyes close. The ears open. It begins with listening.

Then, if you like, cover your eyes the way the custom does, say them again from memory, and sit a breath or two behind your hand, listening. If you pray, you can say the whole first line.

1355.title: Blessed are you
1355.hook: baruch atah: why every Jewish blessing opens by speaking straight to God
1355.carry: every blessing speaks to god face to face
1355.howItsDone: Jews say blessings before eating and drinking, over Sabbath candles and wine, and at many other moments; the standard blessing opens with baruch atah, then God's name, read Adonai, and the words for king of the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shema Yisrael: a silent eye, and a dot that moved to the left. Your line: read it yourself. Today, two more words, the ones that open a blessing.

Friday evening, a kitchen. Two candles are lit, and before anyone eats, someone lifts a cup of wine and starts to speak. Then a hand rests on the bread, and someone speaks again. A new fruit in season, a glass of water, thunder outside, new clothes put on for the first time: the prayer book has a blessing for each, and the formula opens the same way. Two words first, over and over, like the first two notes of a song the whole family knows. Baruch atah. Learn to read them, and you'll see them at the top of page after page.
screen: `CANDLES, WINE, BREAD.` → `A BLESSING FOR EACH.` → `THE SAME TWO WORDS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Baruch atah. Turn it four ways. First, baruch. Bet, with a dot inside so it says b, not v, and the T-shaped mark under it: ba. Resh, then a vav with a dot in its belly, which says oo: ru. At the end, the long-tailed final chaf, one of the five endings, a breathy ch. Ba, ruch. Baruch. Blessed. Second, atah. Alef, silent, carrying a short line: ah. Tav, with a dot inside and the T-shaped mark: ta. Then heh, silent at the end of the word. A, tah. Atah. You. Third, who "you" is. The words are already in Psalm 119: "Blessed art Thou, O LORD; teach me Thy statutes." After baruch atah comes the name of God, which isn't read as written: in prayer it's said Adonai, and outside prayer some say Hashem, the Name. Then come the words for our God, king of the world. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, records two teachers' views: a blessing without the Name is not a blessing, and a blessing without God's kingship is not a blessing. Fourth, a turn some readers notice. Baruch atah speaks straight to God: you. But the blessing over bread goes on, hamotzi, who brings forth bread from the earth, and moves from speaking to God to speaking about God. Close and far in a single sentence. The blessing begins face to face.

1356.title: The root of learning
1356.hook: most Hebrew words grow from a root of three letters
1356.carry: talmud, student, teacher: one root, learning
1356.howItsDone: Students of Hebrew learn to find the three-letter root of a word, and dictionaries of biblical Hebrew are often arranged by root rather than by spelling.

segments.voice: Yesterday, baruch atah: blessed are you, the opening of a blessing. Your line: every blessing speaks to God face to face. Today the alphabet is behind us, and we go underground, to the roots.
screen: `EVERY BLESSING SPEAKS TO GOD FACE TO FACE.`

segments.voice: A student, a teacher, the Talmud, and an hour of study. Four things that seem to have nothing in common. One sits at a desk. One stands at the front. One fills a long shelf of heavy volumes. One is the time you set aside to open a book. Say them in Hebrew and listen: talmid, melamed, Talmud, limud. The same three sounds keep surfacing, l, m, d, like one family face in a row of old photographs. That's how Hebrew is built: three letters underneath, and a whole family of words growing out of them.
screen: `A STUDENT, A TEACHER, A SHELF, A STUDY.` → `TALMID, MELAMED, TALMUD, LIMUD.` → `THE SAME FAMILY FACE.`

segments.voice: Shoresh: a root. Four ways in. First, the idea. A great many Hebrew words grow from a root of three consonants carrying a core meaning. Vowels, and letters added before, after or between, turn it into a noun, a verb, a person, a place. Second, a root you've already met. Lamed, mem, dalet carries learning. Lamad: he learned. Talmid: a student, one who learns. Melamed: a teacher, one who makes others learn. Talmud: the great body of study. In Deuteronomy, Moses tells the people to hear the laws "that ye may learn them," and the Hebrew for learn is built on those same letters. Third, a second root. Kaf, tav, vet carries writing. Katav: he wrote. Michtav: a letter you'd mail. Ktav: handwriting. And Ketuvim, the Writings, the third part of the Hebrew Bible: the Psalms, Proverbs and Ruth. Fourth, the picture in the word itself. Shoresh is the root of a tree. In Jeremiah, the one who trusts in God is like a tree planted by water, sending its roots out toward the stream. You see branches, leaves and fruit; the root stays underground, holding it all together. For the next stretch of the path, we'll dig up one root a day and watch what grows out of it.

segments.voice: Say these slowly and listen for the three sounds that stay: lamad, talmid, melamed, Talmud, l, m, d; then katav, michtav, Ketuvim, k, t, v. Let the words fall away and keep only the three letters, the way a root stays in the ground while the leaves come and go. If you pray, you can do the same with a word from a prayer you know.

1357.title: Sh-L-M
1357.hook: shalom, shalem (whole), shilem (paid): peace means wholeness
1357.howItsDone: Jewish teaching connects shalom, peace, with shalem, whole, and the laws of the Torah require paying back what was damaged or borrowed; shalom is also the everyday greeting and a word that closes many prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shoresh, the three letters under a family of words. Your line: three-letter roots. Today, the first root, under a word you already read.

A receipt stamped paid. A coffee mug with no chips in it. A man limping home after a long, hard night, finally arriving in one piece. And a greeting used coming in and going out. In English they have nothing in common. In Hebrew, the same three letters: shin, lamed, mem. A few days ago you read shalom letter by letter and stopped there. Today we lift out the root, and it turns out to be bigger than the word you thought you knew.
screen: `A RECEIPT STAMPED PAID.` → `A MUG WITH NO CHIPS.` → `HOME IN ONE PIECE.` → `ONE ROOT: SH-L-M.`

segments.voice: Sh-L-M. Four ways in. First, shalem: whole, complete, nothing missing. In Deuteronomy, a merchant is told to keep a weight that is shelemah, whole, and tzedek, just: no shaving a little off when the customer isn't looking. A whole weight is an honest one. Second, shilem: to pay, to make good. In the laws of Exodus, when someone damages what belongs to a neighbor, the Hebrew says he must make it whole, with a verb from this root: restitution, paying it back until nothing is missing. Third, the man limping home. In Genesis, after Jacob wrestles all night and leaves limping, after he meets the brother he feared, the text says he arrived shalem at the city of Shechem. The commentator Rashi reads it three ways: whole in his body, healed; whole in his possessions, even after the gifts he gave away; whole in his learning, having forgotten nothing in his long years away. Fourth, shalom. Read through its root, peace isn't only the absence of a fight. It's wholeness: nothing owed, nothing broken, nothing missing. A home at peace is a home where things are whole between people. When people greet each other with shalom, they may be wishing far more than quiet. Paying what you owe is one way of making something whole.
screen: `SHALEM: A WHOLE, HONEST WEIGHT.` · `SHILEM: PAY IT BACK, MAKE IT WHOLE.` · `JACOB ARRIVES SHALEM.` · `SHALOM: NOTHING OWED, NOTHING MISSING.` · then, large: `PEACE IS WHOLENESS.`

segments.voice: Let your mind look for one small thing still open: a text you owe a reply, a little money borrowed from a friend, a book never returned, a thank you you meant to say. Hold it and notice how it sits, slightly unfinished, then breathe in and feel what whole might be like. If you pray, you can hold that one thing in your prayer.
Sh-L-M. Shin, lamed, mem: the root of shalom, peace; shalem, whole; and shilem, paid. Today's word.
Your line: peace is wholeness. Paying back can be a kind of peace. That's today, done.

1358.title: B-R-K
1358.hook: bracha (blessing), berech (knee), breichah (pool): blessing bends and flows
1358.howItsDone: In the Amidah, worshippers bend the knees at the word baruch, bow at atah, and straighten before God's name; the Hebrew words for blessing and knee are listed under the same three letters, b-r-k.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sh-L-M: shalom, shalem, shilem, and your line: peace is wholeness. Today, the root under baruch, and the end of the week.

Evening, outside a town, at a well. A servant has walked a long way with ten camels, sent to find a wife for his master's son. Before he asks anything of anyone, he brings the camels down onto their knees beside the water. In Hebrew, the verb for making them kneel is built on bet, resh, kaf, the same three letters as baruch, the first word of a blessing. Only then does the servant pray. The root of blessing, down in the dust beside the water.
screen: `A WELL AT EVENING.` → `THE CAMELS KNEEL.` → `THE SAME LETTERS AS BARUCH.`

segments.voice: B-R-K. Four ways in. First, bracha: a blessing. Baruch, blessed, from three days ago, grows from these letters. Second, berech: a knee. In Psalm 95, the call to worship says "let us kneel before the LORD," and the Hebrew for kneel is from this root. In the Amidah, the standing prayer, a custom traced to the Talmud has people bend the knees at baruch, bow at atah, and stand straight again for God's name. The body says the word. Third, breichah: a pool, water gathered low where the ground bends down to hold it. Dictionaries list the knee and the blessing under the same letters. Whether they began as one word is a question for linguists. But some readers hear them together: blessing is something you bend toward, and something that pools and flows. Fourth, the week behind you. It began with dots, the nikud that give letters a voice. Then your first word, shalom. Then the Shema's first two words, a silent eye and a dot that moved. Then baruch atah. Then shoresh, the root under the word, and the first root, sh-l-m, peace as wholeness. And now b-r-k, the root under the blessing you learned to read. A week ago these were single letters. Now they're words you can sound out, and roots you can dig up.
screen: `BRACHA: A BLESSING.` · `BERECH: THE KNEE THAT BENDS.` · `BREICHAH: WATER GATHERED LOW.` · `THE WEEK: DOTS, WORDS, ROOTS.` · then, large: `BLESSING BENDS.`

segments.voice: If you're able, stand; sitting is fine too. Bring to mind one thing from this week you're grateful for, small and real, and slowly let your knees bend a little, the way the custom bends at baruch, then straighten, or if you're seated, bow your head and lift it. Once is enough; then sit and let the thanks pool, and if you pray, you can say baruch atah as you bend.
B-R-K. Bet, resh, kaf: the root of bracha, blessing, sitting beside berech, knee, and breichah, pool. Today's word.
Your line: blessing bends. Thanks can gather low, like water. That's a week of reading.
